tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: athena-finance is Eric's private finance and investing webapp, built on Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Supabase, and Tailwind/shadcn UI. CLAUDE.md is the real orientation document here (the auto-generated README is just create-next-app boilerplate) â€” it lays out the tech stack, project structure (src/app for routes, supabase/ for schema and migrations), and working rules like TypeScript strict mode and Supabase Row Level Security. Keep its domain map in mind: everyday finance (accounts, transactions, contracts, debts, goals), plus distinctive subsystems for crypto/Kraken, bank-sync automation, German tax, and an AI assistant â€” this tour visits each in turn.

tour.title: Authentication & Session Handling
tour.description: Every request flows through src/proxy.ts, the Next.js middleware that refreshes Supabase auth tokens on the edge and enforces protected routes â€” this is the first code a request touches. It relies on two Supabase client factories: server.ts (used in Server Components and Server Actions, with the highest fan-in of any file in the codebase at 73 dependents) and client.ts (for browser-side access). Login itself is a Server Action in src/app/login/actions.ts, which signs in/up/out and reports errors via redirect query params rather than client-side state.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js middleware (proxy.ts here, historically named middleware.ts) runs on the Edge Runtime before a request reaches a page â€” it can read/write cookies but cannot use most Node APIs, which is why Supabase's @supabase/ssr package exists: it keeps the auth cookie in sync between edge middleware, server components, and the browser.

tour.title: Dashboard Shell & Navigation
tour.description: Once authenticated, src/app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx wraps every protected page: it re-checks the session server-side and preloads the user's profile, settings, and Athena assistant configuration in one pass. The actual chrome is a Client Component, app-shell.tsx, which manages the mobile drawer/backdrop state and switches between a fixed desktop sidebar and a slide-out mobile one (sidebar.tsx) â€” the mobile-first responsive patterns documented in the project's own conventions.
tour.languageLesson: React Server/Client Component split: layout.tsx stays a Server Component so it can await Supabase queries directly, while app-shell.tsx is marked 'use client' only where interactivity (drawer open/close, usePathname) is actually needed â€” pushing 'use client' as far down the tree as possible keeps more of the app server-rendered.

tour.title: Shared Foundations: Types, Formatting, Settings
tour.description: Three files underpin almost the entire app. src/types/database.ts is the auto-generated Supabase schema â€” it has the highest fan-out in the codebase (92 files import from it) because every feature's data shape derives from these table types. src/lib/format.ts (currency/number/date formatting) and src/lib/settings.ts (server-side profile/settings fetching) are the next most depended-upon utilities, used everywhere from dashboards to tax reports for consistent, locale-aware output.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript types generated straight from the Postgres schema (via the Supabase CLI) give end-to-end type safety: a column rename in a migration shows up as a compile error everywhere that column is read, instead of failing silently at runtime.

tour.title: Everyday Finance: Dashboard & Accounts
tour.description: This is the app's home base. dashboard/page.tsx aggregates net worth, recent activity, and widgets from every domain (crypto, depot, bank) into one view, while finance/accounts/page.tsx â€” the single highest fan-out page in the app (46 imports) â€” manages the bank/cash/investment accounts that everything else (transactions, contracts, debts, goals) is scoped to. Together they show the 'everyday' finance domain that the more specialized subsystems in the next steps plug into.

tour.title: Bank Sync: FinTS Automation
tour.description: Rather than manual entry, athena-finance pulls real German bank data via the FinTS protocol. src/lib/fints/index.ts orchestrates the sync and data mapping in TypeScript, but delegates the actual protocol handshake to sidecar.ts, which shells out to a Python subprocess (the fints library isn't available for Node) â€” a genuinely polyglot piece of the stack. categorize.ts then runs a learning categorization engine over the imported transactions, and api/bank/sync/route.ts plus the cron/bank-sync route expose this manually and on a schedule.
tour.languageLesson: Polyglot serverless functions: this project ships both TypeScript and Python (requirements.txt/scripts/fints) in the same Vercel deployment. The Node side calls the Python sidecar as a child process because the mature FinTS/HBCI client library is Python-only â€” a pragmatic escape hatch instead of reimplementing a banking protocol in TypeScript.

tour.title: Database Schema: Bank Data & Unified Transactions
tour.description: The bank_integration migration introduces the bank_transactions and bank_balance tables that Step 6's FinTS sync writes into. Because the app also has manually-entered transactions from the core finance domain, the later unify_finance_banking migration adds a unified_transactions SQL view that merges both sources with a consistent signed-amount and flow-kind shape â€” so pages like the dashboard (Step 5) can query one interface regardless of where a transaction actually came from.
tour.languageLesson: SQL views as an integration layer: instead of every page needing to know about two separate transaction tables, a view (unified_transactions) presents a single read-only interface. It's recomputed on each query rather than stored, so it always reflects the latest rows in both underlying tables â€” at some query-cost trade-off versus a materialized table.

tour.title: Crypto Portfolio & Kraken Rebalancing
tour.description: The crypto/Kraken integration is a self-contained domain layer: src/lib/kraken/index.ts talks to the Kraken exchange REST API for balances, tickers, and trade history, while server actions in crypto/actions.ts (29 outgoing dependencies, one of the app's broadest files) tie that data into Supabase-backed portfolio state. On top of the raw holdings sits src/lib/crypto/rebalancing.ts, a calculation engine that compares current allocation against target percentages across multiple portfolios and flags trades needed to rebalance â€” surfaced on the crypto page and refreshed by a dedicated cron sync.

tour.title: German Tax Engine (ESt & EÃœR)
tour.description: src/lib/tax is a small but dense rules engine for German income tax: tarif.ts implements the progressive tax formula itself (estFuerZvE â€” tax owed for a given taxable income), position.ts derives a tax position from booked transactions, and euer.ts handles the EinnahmenÃ¼berschussrechnung (simplified profit/loss statement required for freelancers). These feed the steuer/page.tsx overview and the steuer/euer/page.tsx report â€” a good example of business-domain logic that lives entirely in src/lib, decoupled from any UI.
tour.languageLesson: Domain logic named in the domain's own language (zvE, estRoh, EÃœR) rather than translated to generic English â€” a deliberate choice here since the rules only make sense relative to German tax law (Einkommensteuergesetz), and translating the vocabulary would make it harder to cross-check against the actual statute.

tour.title: Athena AI Assistant
tour.description: Athena is a chat assistant that can read and write the user's financial data and render charts inline. api/assistant/route.ts is the streaming chat endpoint (18 outgoing dependencies), src/lib/assistant/tools.ts defines the tool-calling functions Athena can invoke against financial data, and prompts.ts builds its system prompt and context. On the frontend, AthenaChat.tsx drives the conversation UI while AthenaChart.tsx lets model responses render live charts instead of just text â€” tying the assistant back into the same data model covered in Steps 4-9.
tour.languageLesson: Tool-calling (function calling) architecture: instead of the LLM directly touching the database, it emits structured calls to a fixed set of functions defined in tools.ts (e.g. 'get transactions', 'create contract'); the server validates and executes them, then feeds results back to the model. This keeps the assistant's actions auditable and bounded to an explicit API surface rather than free-form code execution.

tour.title: Reports & Scheduled Automation
tour.description: Closing the loop, src/lib/reports/build.ts aggregates transaction history, category breakdowns, and net-worth changes into a report â€” the same kind of cross-domain synthesis the dashboard (Step 5) does, but exported as a document via the monthly-report cron route. vercel.json is where all of this automation is actually wired up: it defines the scheduled cron jobs for bank sync, Kraken sync, and monthly reports seen throughout this tour, tying the FinTS, crypto, and tax/report subsystems together as recurring background jobs rather than on-demand actions.
tour.languageLesson: Vercel Cron Jobs are declared declaratively in vercel.json (path + schedule expression) rather than in code â€” Vercel's platform calls the given route on schedule, so the route handler itself just needs to authenticate the cron trigger and run like any other request.
